title: Non-blocking stdio serving (coexist with an event loop)
description:
The stdio transport blocks the process in `nanonext::wait(cv)`, so a server that also needs to run a {later}/httpuv event loop (e.g. a live Shiny app speaking MCP over stdio to Claude Desktop) can't use it.

Shiny's dependency-free workaround: `file(\"stdin\", blocking = FALSE)` polled from a `later::later()` loop (Unix only; see `R/mcp-stdio.R` on the shiny branch). nanonext's `read_stdin()` could support the same pattern if exposed as a pollable/aio rather than a blocking loop.

_Part of #115._

title: Expose an embeddable JSON-RPC dispatch (mount into an existing httpuv app)
description:
`mcp_server()` owns its process: stdio blocks on a nanonext cv loop, HTTP starts its own `httpuv::startServer()` + `service(Inf)`, and `check_not_interactive()` forbids embedding. Frameworks that already run httpuv (shiny, plumber2, ambiorix) can't mount an mcptools endpoint on their existing port/event loop.

Suggested shape:

```r
dispatch <- mcp_dispatch(tools = ..., resources = ...)
# function(body, req = NULL) -> JSON-RPC response list | promise | NULL (notification)
```

with `mcp_server()` becoming a thin stdio/HTTP wrapper around it.

_Part of #115._

title: Support async tool handlers (promises)
description:
`execute_tool_call()` is synchronous and the HTTP transport returns plain lists from the httpuv `call`. Tools that need to wait (long-poll patterns, external requests via {promises}) can't be expressed.

httpuv already supports returning a promise from `call`; if a tool handler returns a promise, mcptools could chain the JSON-RPC response onto it. Shiny's MCP tunnel depends on this (a receive tool holds its response until the app has messages to flush).

_Part of #115._

title: Support tool _meta in tools/list responses
description:
`tool_as_json()` emits name/title/description/inputSchema/annotations only; there is no way to attach `_meta` to a served tool.

MCP Apps requires `_meta.ui.resourceUri` on the tool that opens the app, and `_meta.ui.visibility: [\"app\"]` on tools that only the iframe (not the model) may call. ellmer's tool annotations have no slot for arbitrary `_meta`.

Suggested shape: a `meta` argument when registering tools (or honoring a `_meta` field on ellmer tool annotations), passed through verbatim in `tools/list`.

_Part of #115._

title: Support MCP resources (resources/list, resources/read)
description:
`capabilities()` advertises `resources`, but `resources/list` and `resources/read` fall through to `Method not found` in both transports (`handle_http_request_message()` / `handle_message_from_client()` in `R/server.R`).

Resources are required for MCP Apps (the `ui://` HTML is delivered via `resources/read`), and generally useful for serving files/data to hosts.

Suggested shape: `mcp_resource(uri, mime_type, handler, meta = NULL)` accepted by `mcp_server()` alongside tools, where `handler()` returns the contents (text or raw).

_Part of #115._

title: Serving MCP Apps: gaps for embedding mcptools in other frameworks (tracking)
description:
[Shiny is growing experimental support](https://github.com/rstudio/shiny) for serving apps as [MCP Apps (SEP-1865)](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps): an MCP endpoint mounted on the app's own httpuv server whose `ui://` resource renders the live app in the host's sandboxed iframe.

The original plan was to build that endpoint on {mcptools}. That wasn't possible with v1.0.0 / current dev, so shiny currently carries a minimal internal JSON-RPC endpoint. This issue collects the gaps as sub-issues so the implementations can converge — ideally shiny (and other embedders like plumber) could eventually delegate protocol handling to {mcptools}.

Each sub-issue is independently useful; none is MCP-Apps-specific except the tool `_meta` one.

Shiny's internal implementation (a reference for what embedders need): `R/mcp-server.R`, `R/mcp-tunnel.R`, `R/mcp-stdio.R` on the [`schloerke/shiny-mcp-app-protocol` branch](https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/tree/schloerke/shiny-mcp-app-protocol).

## Parts

- [ ] #116 (resources/list + resources/read)
- [ ] #117 (tool `_meta` in tools/list)
- [ ] #118 (async tool handlers via promises)
- [ ] #119 (embeddable JSON-RPC dispatch)
- [ ] #120 (non-blocking stdio serving)

title: Consider non-tool elements with `mcp_tools()`
description:
Follow-up to #108.

On the server-side, `mcp_server()` gives us a broader entry point to support other content types, like prompts / instructions. We could just add an argument if we wanted to support those.

On the client-side, the `mcp_tools()` interface might paint us into a corner. The function is named `mcp_tools()` and is documented as returning a list that can be provided directly to `ellmer::Chat$register_tools()`. It's possible that the use cases of e.g. Notion / Atlassian / Databricks MCP servers we're imagining might end up needing to interface with the prompts / instructions fields. Probably worth waiting to give a go at that until we really have a need, though—it might be the case that really everything substantive lives in tools.

title: Tool title field not supported (MCP spec 2025-06-18)
description:
## Problem

The MCP spec (2025-06-18) defines an optional [`title`](https://spec.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools/) field on tool definitions — a human-readable display name separate from the `name` identifier.

`tool_as_json()` only serializes `name`, `description`, and `inputSchema`. The `title` field is omitted.

## Why This Matters

- `name` is a programmatic identifier (e.g., `"query_occurrences_ala"`)
- `title` is a human-readable display name (e.g., `"Query ALA Occurrences"`)
- `description` is the detailed explanation for the LLM

Clients use `title` in UI elements like tool pickers and confirmation dialogs. Without it, clients fall back to showing `name` (ugly) or `description` (verbose).

## Expected

```r
ellmer::tool(
  fun = function() "...",
  name = "query_occurrences_ala",
  title = "Query ALA Occurrences",
  description = "Search the Atlas of Living Australia for species occurrence records"
)
```

Should produce:
```json
{
  "name": "query_occurrences_ala",
  "title": "Query ALA Occurrences",
  "description": "Search the Atlas of Living Australia...",
  "inputSchema": {...}
}
```

## Fix

1. Add `title` parameter to `ellmer::tool()` (stores on ToolDef)
2. Include in `tool_as_json()` output when present

Lower priority than #103 and #104 but straightforward to implement alongside them.

title: No support for structuredContent in tool results (MCP spec 2025-06-18)
description:
## Problem

The MCP spec (2025-06-18) defines a [`structuredContent`](https://spec.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools/#structured-content) field on tool results — a JSON object that provides machine-readable structured output alongside the human-readable `content` text.

Currently, `as_tool_call_result()` only produces `content` (text-only). There's no path for `structuredContent`.

## Expected

When a tool returns a list/data structure, the result should include both:

```json
{
  "content": [
    {"type": "text", "text": "{\"auc\": 0.92, \"tss\": 0.81}"}
  ],
  "structuredContent": {
    "auc": 0.92,
    "tss": 0.81
  }
}
```

- `content`: Human-readable text (for backwards compatibility)
- `structuredContent`: Machine-readable JSON (for clients that support it)

Per spec: "For backwards compatibility, a tool that returns structured content SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a TextContent block."

## Use Case

SDM MCP server with ~70 tools. Each tool produces structured results (model metrics, file paths, area statistics). Clients that understand `structuredContent` get validated, typed data. Others fall back to text. This is the biggest quality-of-life improvement for tool-heavy servers.

## Fix

In `as_tool_call_result()`, if the tool result is a list (and not an ellmer Content object), include it as `structuredContent` alongside the text serialization.

Related to #103 (outputSchema) — if a tool declares an outputSchema, the structuredContent should be validated against it.

title: No support for tool outputSchema (MCP spec 2025-06-18)
description:
## Problem

The MCP spec (2025-06-18) defines an [`outputSchema`](https://spec.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools/#output-schema) field on tool definitions — a JSON Schema describing the expected structure of tool results. This enables clients to validate outputs and provides type information for better integration.

Neither `tool_as_json()` nor `ellmer::tool()` currently support declaring an output schema.

## Expected

```r
ellmer::tool(
  fun = function() list(auc = 0.92, tss = 0.81),
  name = "evaluate_model",
  description = "Evaluate model performance",
  arguments = list(),
  outputSchema = list(
    type = "object",
    properties = list(
      auc = list(type = "number"),
      tss = list(type = "number")
    ),
    required = c("auc", "tss")
  )
)
```

Should produce in `tools/list`:
```json
{
  "name": "evaluate_model",
  "description": "Evaluate model performance",
  "inputSchema": {...},
  "outputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "auc": {"type": "number"},
      "tss": {"type": "number"}
    },
    "required": ["auc", "tss"]
  }
}
```

## Use Case

Building an SDM MCP server with ~70 tools. Each tool returns structured data (metrics, file paths, statistics). `outputSchema` would let clients validate every tool response automatically instead of parsing free-form text.

## Fix

1. Add `outputSchema` parameter to `ellmer::tool()` (stores on ToolDef)
2. Include in `tool_as_json()` output in mcptools

Depends on ellmer changes first, then mcptools serialization.

title: tool_as_json() omits annotations field from tools/list response
description:
## Problem

`tool_as_json()` in `R/server.R` serializes tool definitions for the `tools/list` MCP response, but only includes `name`, `description`, and `inputSchema` — it omits the `annotations` field entirely.

The [MCP specification (2025-03-26+)](https://spec.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/server/tools/#tool-annotations) defines tool annotations as part of each tool's definition in `tools/list`. ellmer already supports declaring them via `tool(annotations = tool_annotations(...))` and stores them on the `ToolDef` S7 object. mcptools just doesn't include them in the JSON response.

## Current Code

```r
# R/server.R, line 479
tool_as_json <- function(tool) {
  # ... inputSchema computation ...
  list(
    name = tool@name,
    description = tool@description,
    inputSchema = inputSchema
    # annotations: missing
  )
}
```

## Expected MCP Response

```json
{
  "name": "draw_random",
  "description": "Draw random numbers",
  "inputSchema": { ... },
  "annotations": {
    "readOnlyHint": true,
    "idempotentHint": true,
    "openWorldHint": false
  }
}
```

## Fix

One line addition in `tool_as_json()`:

```r
list(
  name = tool@name,
  description = tool@description,
  inputSchema = inputSchema,
  annotations = if (length(tool@annotations)) tool@annotations else NULL
)
```

This is backwards-compatible — tools without annotations get `annotations: null` (or omitted if the client filters nulls), which is the same as current behaviour.

## Use Case

We're building an SDM (species distribution modelling) MCP server with ~70 tools. Some are read-only queries, some are destructive (delete project), some make network calls. Tool annotations let MCP clients show appropriate confirmation prompts and enforce safety — but they're silently dropped today.

Happy to open a PR for this.

## Environment
- mcptools 0.2.1
- ellmer 0.3.x

title: Claude Code ↔ RStudio MCP bridge hangs silently — enterprise security blocks IPC sockets, TCP fix included
description:
Claude Code ↔ RStudio MCP bridge hangs silently — enterprise security blocks IPC sockets, TCP fix included

## Problem

When `session_tools = TRUE` (the default), all `tools/call` requests (except `list_r_sessions` / `select_r_session`) are forwarded to a connected R session via `forward_request()`. The forwarded call never returns — the MCP server hangs indefinitely with no error or timeout.

Setting `session_tools = FALSE` and executing tools locally in the MCP server process works perfectly.

## Environment

- macOS 26.4 (Tahoe), Apple Silicon
- R 4.5.2
- mcptools 0.2.1 (CRAN)
- btw 1.2.1 (CRAN)
- nanonext (current CRAN version)
- Claude Code 2.1.92 as MCP client
- Palo Alto Cortex XDR endpoint security extension active (may be relevant — see below)

## Reproduction

1. Register MCP server: `Rscript -e 'btw::btw_mcp_server()'`
2. In RStudio, run `btw::btw_mcp_session()`
3. From the MCP client, call any btw tool (e.g. `btw_tool_sessioninfo_platform`)
4. The call hangs forever. No response on stdout, no error on stderr. User has to interrupt call.

`list_r_sessions` works because it is excluded from forwarding in `handle_message_from_client()`.

## Diagnostic methodology

### 1. Wrapper script to capture stdin/stdout

Created a bash wrapper that logs both sides of the MCP stdio transport:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
LOG="$HOME/Desktop/btw_debug.log"

# Capture stdin (what the client sends TO the server)
tee -a "${LOG}.stdin" < /dev/stdin > "$FIFO" &

# Run server, capture stdout (what the server sends BACK)
Rscript -e 'btw::btw_mcp_server()' \
  < "$FIFO" \
  > >(tee -a "${LOG}.stdout") \
  2> >(tee -a "${LOG}.stderr" >&2)
```

**Result:** stdin log confirmed tool calls were reaching the server. stdout log showed responses for `initialize` (id=0), `tools/list` (id=1), `prompts/list` error (id=2), `resources/list` error (id=3), and `list_r_sessions` (id=4) — but **zero output** for `btw_tool_sessioninfo_platform` (id=5). The server received the request but never wrote a response.

### 2. FIFO-based MCP protocol simulation

Sent JSON-RPC messages manually to isolate the server from the MCP client:

```bash
FIFO=$(mktemp -u); mkfifo "$FIFO"
Rscript -e "btw::btw_mcp_server()" < "$FIFO" > out.txt 2> err.txt &
exec 3>"$FIFO"

# Send initialize
echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"test","version":"1.0"}}}' >&3
sleep 3
echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' >&3
sleep 2

# Send tool call
echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"btw_tool_sessioninfo_platform","arguments":{"_intent":"test"}}}' >&3
sleep 5

exec 3>&-
```

**Result:** Same behaviour — initialize responded, tool call produced no output.

### 3. Event loop liveness test

After the hung tool call, sent a `tools/list` request to check if the server was still alive:

```bash
# After tool call hangs...
echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":99,"method":"tools/list"}' >&3
```

**Result:** `tools/list` (id=99) responded immediately. The event loop is alive and processing messages — only the forwarded tool call is silently dropped.

### 4. Runtime patching to trace dispatch

Patched `handle_message_from_client` at startup to log the forwarding decision:

```r
original_handler <- mcptools:::handle_message_from_client
assignInNamespace("handle_message_from_client", function(line) {
  data <- tryCatch(jsonlite::parse_json(line), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(data) && identical(data$method, "tools/call")) {
    env <- mcptools:::the
    message("[CHECK] sessions_enabled: ", env$sessions_enabled)
    pipes_val <- nanonext::stat(env$server_socket, "pipes")
    message("[CHECK] pipes: ", pipes_val)
    local_exec <- !env$sessions_enabled || 
      data$params$name %in% c("list_r_sessions", "select_r_session") || 
      !nanonext::stat(env$server_socket, "pipes")
    message("[CHECK] would execute locally: ", local_exec)
  }
  original_handler(line)
}, "mcptools")
```

**Result:**
```
[CHECK] sessions_enabled: TRUE
[CHECK] pipes: 1
[CHECK] would execute locally: FALSE
```

Confirmed: the tool call is being forwarded (not executed locally) because `sessions_enabled = TRUE` and `pipes = 1`.

### 5. Tracing tool dispatch functions

Patched `execute_tool_call`, `call_tool`, `mcp_request_tool_call`, and `as_tool_call_result` — **none were called** during the forwarded tool call. This confirms the request goes into `forward_request()` -> `nanonext::send_aio()` and the response path via `handle_message_from_session()` never fires.

### 6. Direct function test

Called the tool function directly outside the MCP server:

```r
x <- btw::btw_tool_sessioninfo_platform()
print(x)
# Works perfectly, returns in <1 second
```

The tool itself is fine — the issue is exclusively in the nanonext IPC forwarding path.

## Analysis of the forwarding code

In `mcp_server_stdio()`, when `sessions_enabled = TRUE`:

```r
the$server_socket <- nanonext::socket("poly")
nanonext::dial(the$server_socket, url = sprintf("%s%d", the$socket_url, 1L))
```

The server dials to `ipc:///tmp/mcptools-socket1`. On the RStudio side, `mcp_session()` listens on the same address. The connection is established (`pipes = 1`).

`forward_request()` calls `append_tool_fn(data)` to attach the R tool function to the request, then sends via `nanonext::send_aio(the$server_socket, prepared, mode = "serial")`.

On the RStudio side, the receive handler is promise-based:

```r
the$raio <- nanonext::recv_aio(the$session_socket, mode = "serial")
promises::as.promise(the$raio)$then(handle_message_from_server)$catch(function(e) {})
```

The empty `.catch(function(e) {})` silently swallows any error.

## Evidence pointing to nanonext IPC as the issue

As a control test, we installed [ClaudeR](https://github.com/imnmv/clauder) — an alternative MCP server that connects to the same live R session but uses **HTTP on localhost:8787** (via httpuv) instead of nanonext Unix domain sockets. ClaudeR's `execute_r("ls()")` immediately returned the objects in the R session's global environment. This confirms:

- The R session is responsive and accessible
- The MCP client (Claude Code) is working correctly
- The issue is specifically the nanonext IPC socket transport, not the R session, IDE, or MCP protocol

## Possible causes

1. **Endpoint security software (most likely)** — This machine runs Palo Alto Cortex XDR with an Endpoint Security Extension (`TrapsSecurityExtension`). This hooks into macOS's Endpoint Security Framework and monitors IPC. The nanonext socket files at `/tmp/mcptools-socket*` are created and the connection appears established, but data may not flow through. The fact that HTTP localhost works (ClaudeR) while Unix domain sockets don't (mcptools) is consistent with endpoint security selectively blocking IPC socket communication. I was unable to fully disable Cortex XDR to confirm.

2. **Promise resolution in RStudio** — The `recv_aio` promise on the RStudio side may not be resolving. If `later` is not actively polling the nanonext aio, the message is never received.

3. **Silent error in `.catch`** — If deserialization of the forwarded request fails on the RStudio side, the empty catch handler drops the error and `handle_message_from_server` is never called, so no response is sent.

## Suggestions

- **Add a `transport` option to `mcp_server()` / `mcp_session()`** — e.g. `transport = c("ipc", "tcp", "http")`. The current nanonext IPC transport (`ipc:///tmp/mcptools-socket*`) is blocked by some enterprise endpoint security software. A TCP (`tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT`) or HTTP (`httpuv`) alternative would let users on managed machines switch transports without abandoning session bridging entirely. This could be as simple as:
  ```r
  mcp_server(session_tools = TRUE, transport = "tcp")  # uses tcp://127.0.0.1:PORT instead of ipc://
  mcp_session(transport = "tcp")
  ```
- **Add a timeout to `forward_request()`** — if no response comes back within N seconds, return an error to the MCP client instead of hanging forever.
- **Log errors in the `.catch` handler** — `function(e) { message("[mcptools] session error: ", conditionMessage(e)) }` would make debugging much easier.
- **Add a diagnostic mode** — e.g. `mcp_session(verbose = TRUE)` to log when messages are received and responses are sent on the RStudio side.

## Workaround (full fix — TCP transport)

The issue is specifically with Unix domain sockets (`ipc://`). Switching to TCP localhost restores full session bridging, including live environment inspection. The fix patches `the$socket_url` on both the server and session sides before startup.

**MCP server side** — save as e.g. `~/.claude/r-btw-server.R` and register with Claude Code:

```r
library(mcptools)
ns <- asNamespace("mcptools")
unlockBinding("the", ns)
the_env <- get("the", envir = ns)
the_env$socket_url <- "tcp://127.0.0.1:4777"
btw::btw_mcp_server()
```

```bash
claude mcp add -s "user" r-btw -- Rscript --vanilla ~/.claude/r-btw-server.R
```

**R session side** — add to `.Rprofile` so it runs automatically:

```r
# Patch mcptools to use TCP instead of IPC (bypasses endpoint security blocking Unix sockets)
if (interactive() && requireNamespace("mcptools", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ns <- asNamespace("mcptools")
  unlockBinding("the", ns)
  the_env <- get("the", envir = ns)
  the_env$socket_url <- "tcp://127.0.0.1:4777"
  btw::btw_mcp_session()
}
```

**Confirmed working:** After this patch, `btw_tool_env_describe_data_frame` and `btw_tool_env_describe_environment` successfully return objects from the live RStudio session. The TCP transport is not blocked by Palo Alto Cortex XDR.

**Control test:** [ClaudeR](https://github.com/imnmv/clauder), which uses HTTP on localhost:8787 (httpuv) instead of nanonext, also worked immediately — further confirming the issue is specific to Unix domain socket IPC, not the R session or MCP protocol.

## Fallback workaround (no session bridging)

If TCP also doesn't work in your environment:

```bash
claude mcp add -s "user" r-btw -- \
  Rscript -e 'mcptools::mcp_server(tools = btw:::btw_mcp_tools(), session_tools = FALSE)'
```

This executes all tools locally in the MCP server process. Loses live environment inspection but all other tools work correctly.

title: Support non-text content types (images, other) in tool results
description:
## Problem

`as_tool_call_result()` currently hardcodes all tool results as `type: "text"` content blocks:

```r
jsonrpc_response(data$id, list(content = list(list(type = "text", 
    text = format_result(result))), isError = is_error))
```

The [MCP specification](https://spec.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools/#tool-result) supports multiple content types in tool results, including `image` (base64-encoded) and `audio`. There's currently no way for an R tool to return an image that renders inline in the client (e.g., Claude Desktop).

## Use Case

We're building an MCP server for data analysis. Our tool produces plots, such as Kaplan-Meier survival curves and other plots. We'd like to return these plots as inline images so the LLM client can see and reason about them — but today everything gets serialized to text.

## Proposed Behavior

When a tool function returns an `ellmer::ContentImageInline` object (or a list containing one), `as_tool_call_result()` should produce the appropriate MCP image content block:

```json
{
  "content": [
    { "type": "image", "data": "<base64>", "mimeType": "image/png" }
  ]
}
```

Ideally this would also support mixed content (text + image) in a single tool result, which the MCP spec allows.

`ellmer` already has the building blocks: `content_image_file()`, `content_image_plot()`, and `ContentImageInline` — it's just the mcptools serialization layer that doesn't handle them.

## Environment

- mcptools 0.2.1
- ellmer 0.3.2
- R 4.4.x

title: mcp_tools() fails with "system error 232" on Windows when `env` is set in MCP server config
description:
**Description:**
When using `mcp_tools(config = "...")` in **ellmer** with an MCP server configuration that includes an `env` block, the connection immediately fails on Windows with the following error:

```
Error in `process_write_input(self, private, str, sep)`:
! Native call to `processx_connection_write_bytes` failed
Caused by error in `chain_call(c_processx_connection_write_bytes, con, str)`:
! Cannot write connection (system error 232, Идет закрытие канала.
) @processx-connection.c:977 (processx_c_connection_write_bytes)
Type .Last.error to see the more details.
```

If the same configuration is used **without** the `env` key, everything works as expected.

---

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Create a minimal R MCP server script, e.g. `create_pf_mcp_server.R`.
2. Add it to the MCP config **with env**:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "netpeak_pfworker": {
      "command": "Rscript",
      "args": ["-e", "source('C:/Users/User/Documents/mcp_servers/create_pf_mcp_server.R')"],
      "env": {
        "PFW_TOKEN": "00000000111111111xxxx"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

3. Call:

```r
library(ellmer)
library(mcptools)

chat <- ellmer::chat_google_gemini(system_prompt = "Test")
chat$set_tools(mcptools::mcp_tools(config = "C:/path/config.json"))
```

4. Observe the error above.

5. Modify the config to **remove** `env`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "netpeak_pfworker": {
      "command": "Rscript",
      "args": ["-e", "source('C:/Users/User/Documents/mcp_servers/create_pf_mcp_server.R')"]
    }
  }
}
```

6. Run again — works fine.

---

**Expected behavior:**
Passing `env` should merge environment variables with the current process environment (as is common on other platforms), not completely replace them.

**Actual behavior:**
On Windows, `processx` appears to replace the entire environment, which causes the Rscript process to fail almost immediately, breaking the MCP connection.

---

**System info:**

```
other attached packages:
[1] ellmer_0.3.0        mcptools_0.1.0.9000

loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
 [1] coro_1.1.0        R6_2.5.1          magrittr_2.0.3    rappdirs_0.3.3    glue_1.8.0        
 [6] lifecycle_1.0.4   ps_1.8.1          cli_3.6.3         S7_0.2.0          processx_3.8.4    
[11] compiler_4.4.2    rstudioapi_0.17.1 tools_4.4.2       httr2_1.2.1       rlang_1.1.4       
[16] jsonlite_1.8.9
```

Windows 10/11
R 4.x

---

**Notes:**
This looks like a known `processx` behavior on Windows where `env` fully overrides the environment instead of merging it. If this is intentional, `mcp_tools()` might need to explicitly merge the provided `env` with the current `Sys.getenv()` before spawning the process, to ensure required variables like `PATH` and `R_HOME` are preserved.

Seeing as I've just received access to Clause Opus 4.0, I asked it to diagnose the problem from within my same `cline` session. Honestly, the result blew me away: it managed to pinpoint the issue after an entirely self-directed set of diagnostic tests. I asked Claude to draw up a GH issue report for you, which I reproduce in its entirety below...

(We're living in a brave new world.)

Cheers,
G

...


## Summary

The acquaint MCP server throws an error `MCP error -32603: argument 2 is not a vector` when calling tools that have array parameters. This affects multiple tools and appears to be related to how JSON arrays are converted to R vectors in the MCP protocol implementation.

## Environment

- **R Version**: 4.5.0 (2025-04-11)
- **OS**: macOS Sequoia 15.5 (x86_64, darwin20)
- **MCP Client**: VSCode Cline extension v3.17.8-313
- **acquaint package**: (version unknown - not on CRAN)

## MCP Server Configuration

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "r-acquaint": {
      "timeout": 60,
      "command": "Rscript",
      "args": ["-e", "acquaint::mcp_server()"],
      "transportType": "stdio"
    }
  }
}
```

## Minimal Working Example

### Tools That Work (String Parameters)
```javascript
// This works fine
{
  "server_name": "r-acquaint",
  "tool_name": "btw_tool_session_platform_info",
  "arguments": {
    "intent": "Test platform info"
  }
}

// This also works
{
  "server_name": "r-acquaint", 
  "tool_name": "btw_tool_search_packages",
  "arguments": {
    "query": "ggplot2",
    "intent": "Test package search"
  }
}
```

### Tools That Fail (Array Parameters)
```javascript
// This fails with "argument 2 is not a vector"
{
  "server_name": "r-acquaint",
  "tool_name": "btw_tool_session_package_info", 
  "arguments": {
    "packages": ["base"],
    "intent": "Test package info"
  }
}

// This also fails with the same error
{
  "server_name": "r-acquaint",
  "tool_name": "btw_tool_env_describe_environment",
  "arguments": {
    "items": ["ls"],
    "intent": "Test environment description"
  }
}

// Even with special string values in arrays
{
  "server_name": "r-acquaint",
  "tool_name": "btw_tool_session_package_info",
  "arguments": {
    "packages": ["attached"],
    "intent": "Test with special value"
  }
}
```

## Error Details

**Full Error Message:**
```
MCP error -32603: argument 2 is not a vector
```

**Stack Trace:**
```
McpError: MCP error -32603: argument 2 is not a vector
    at Twe._onresponse (/Users/gmcd/.vscode/extensions/asbx.amzn-cline-3.17.8-313/dist/extension.js:7055:102961)
    at _transport.onmessage (/Users/gmcd/.vscode/extensions/asbx.amzn-cline-3.17.8-313/dist/extension.js:7055:100248)
    at Fwe.processReadBuffer (/Users/gmcd/.vscode/extensions/asbx.amzn-cline-3.17.8-313/dist/extension.js:7057:2210)
    at Socket.<anonymous> (/Users/gmcd/.vscode/extensions/asbx.amzn-cline-3.17.8-313/dist/extension.js:7057:1693)
    [... rest of stack trace ...]
```

## Affected Tools

Based on the tool schemas, the following tools are likely affected:

- `btw_tool_session_package_info` (packages parameter)
- `btw_tool_env_describe_environment` (items parameter)
- Any other tools with array-type parameters

## Analysis

The issue appears to be in the serialization/deserialization layer between the MCP protocol and R functions. When JSON arrays are passed through the MCP protocol, they're not being properly converted to R vectors that the underlying R functions expect.

The error message "argument 2 is not a vector" suggests that:
1. The first argument (likely the function name or context) is being passed correctly
2. The second argument (the array parameter) is not being recognized as a vector by R
3. This could be due to the array being passed as a list, JSON object, or other non-vector type

## Reproduction Steps

1. Set up the acquaint MCP server with the configuration above
2. Call any tool with an array parameter (e.g., `btw_tool_session_package_info`)
3. Observe the "argument 2 is not a vector" error
4. Compare with tools that only use string parameters (these work fine)

## Expected Behavior

Array parameters should be properly converted to R vectors before being passed to the underlying R functions, allowing these tools to work correctly.

## Workaround

Currently avoiding tools with array parameters and using only string-parameter tools as a temporary workaround.

description:
There had been some discussion of implementing a `tools` argument for `mcp_server()` that is a list of ellmer tools (the same format as the `.acquaint_tools` option currently is). This would take a default `mcp_server(tools = btw::btw_tools())` (at least until #35  is resolved).

* No `.acquaint_tools` R option to have to know about
* No `mcp_set_tools()` (and thus need to name it informatively) function to configure it

That said, if the user wanted to configure tools other than the default, they'd either 1) have a super long-winded client config or 2) pass an actual script to Rscript that sets up the tools and then calls `mcp_server()` with them in the client config.

This _does_ make things a bit more complicated for the developers, though, as both the server and the sessions need access to those tools. If the tools are defined in the server process and passed as `tools`, the server needs to be able to pass arbitrary R functions to sessions for them to execute rather than just json as strings, as it's currently implemented.

title: distinguishing acquaint and btw
description:
*Written together with @gadenbuie*

Some folks have felt some dissonance with the distinction of btw and acquaint. Leaving some thoughts here, in conversation with Garrick and @hadley, about the way this might look. In short, we want "one place" for end users to go for "give context to LLMs," and clear division of responsibilities if the two packages remain separate.

## Scope of btw and acquaint

Currently, here's what btw and acquaint do:

1) **btw** provides a collection of tools for R users to bring context from their R session to an LLM. The long-term vision for btw is to provide the foundation for agentic workflows for R users.

     a. btw tools are currently mostly context providers -- reading help pages, vignettes, describing objects in the current environment, searching for packages, etc. But we plan to include more R and data-science specific tools in the future, like running code and interacting with SQL databases.
	 
     b. btw is to support a broad collection of entry-points to these tools to make them easy to use in a variety of settings. In addition to the tool definitions and their underlying functions, btw also provides 
	 
      * `btw()` for copying context to the clipboard for manual use in UIs like ChatGPT or Claude;
      * `btw_client()` for quickly setting up an ellmer `chat_*()` client with btw-registered tools;
      * `btw_app()` to create a shinychat-powered app with btw-registered tools.
			
     c. Finally, because these tools are designed to be used in a project setting, btw includes features to help manage btw within a project. Users can create a `btw.md` markdown file (like `claude.md`) in their project that is used to augment the system prompt with context about the project. It also makes it easy to choose a default provider, model and set of tools for `btw_client()` or `btw_app()`. Garrick has plans to add more project features, like a memory tool that can help maintain project context and forward progress between sessions.
	
2) **acquaint** is primarily focused on the interaction between R sessions and MCP clients/servers and there are currently two primary use cases:

     a. **R as an MCP server**: acquaint allows R sessions to be registered as MCP servers, enabling clients like Claude Desktop to discover run tools in those R sessions. acquaint runs one MCP server that routes tool calls to the appropriate R session where the tools are evaluated.
  
      b. **R as an MCP client** (#34): acquaint can also be used to register tools from MCP servers with ellmer, allowing R sessions to interact with other MCP servers via ellmer.

Ideally, we want "one place" for end users to go for "give context to LLMs," and clear division of responsibilities if the two packages remain separate.

## How acquaint currently works

Currently, on the R as an MCP server side:

1) For a given client, like Claude Desktop, there is _one set of tools_ available which can be run in any of the available R sessions. Claude Desktop actually launches `acquaint::mcp_server()` when it starts up, which registers the tools that are available to it.
   - Users can configure those tools by setting an option in their global `.Rprofile`.
   - The client launches acquaint's MCP server, which reports the set of tools to the client.
	 - Currently these tools are static and do not change between R sessions.
2) To connect an R session with Claude Desktop, users call `mcp_session()` in their interactive R session.
   - `mcp_server()` is really a proxy that routes tool calls to sessions where `mcp_session()` was called. It's not called a _proxy_ because that already refers to something else in the MCP protocol.
3) Clients use two acquaint tools to discover and work with specific R sessions:
   - `list_r_sessions()`: Lists the available R sessions.
   - `select_r_session()`: Selects an R session to run tools in. This is remembered by the acquaint MCP server and used to route subsequent tool calls to the selected session.
	 
What makes acquaint so immediately useful is that the tools registered by `mcp_server()` in step 1 are, by default, btw's collection of tools.

## How acquaint and btw could work together

btw's design has always been to provide interfaces with user-pleasing defaults that incorporate btw's tools:

* `btw_client()` is a nice interface for ellmer's `chat_*()` functions with btw-forward defaults.
* `btw_app()` is `shinychat::chat_app()` but with btw on-by-default.

In this same vein, we propose that acquaint handles the MCP server and client interactions and btw provides the btw-batteries-included wrappers:

* acquaint drops btw as a dependency and supplies no default tools (excluding `list_r_sessions()` and `select_r_session()`). `mcp_server()` and `mcp_session()` still exist but aren't very useful on their own. `ellmer::ToolDef` is still the primary interface for defining tools.
* btw then wraps acquaint's API, e.g. `btw_mcp_server()` and `btw_mcp_session()`, with thin wrappers around acquaint's API that include btw's tools by default.

### Naming things

In this framing, acquaint would be the primary package for MCP server/client interactions, while btw would be the package that provides a collection of tools and user-friendly interfaces for R users to interact with those tools.

As a result, we might want to adjust the naming of the packages to better reflect their roles.

* acquaint would take some boring but discoverable name like `mcptools` (`mcp` is unfortunately taken). This package would fit nicely in `r-lib/` as a package that implements MCP server/client interactions.

* Instead of btw, we could keep the name, we could reuse `acquaint`, or we could find a third, new name. This package would fit nicely in `tidyverse/` next to ellmer as a package that provides a collection of tools for R users to interact with LLMs. We (Simon and Garrick) both like acquaint in eliciting "acquainting LLMs with R", but we also like btw, finding it easier to type on a regular basis and think it works well for the package's scope.

----

cc @wch and @shikokuchuo.

title: Supporting "the other direction"
description:
As of now, acquaint allows for _clients_ like Claude Code or Claude Desktop to interface with R sessions via an MCP _server_.

We're also interested in supporting "the other direction," e.g. allowing ellmer chats to act as a client to other, existing MCP servers. Some have sugested this functionality maybe ought to live in acquaint. cc @hadley, @gadenbuie, https://github.com/tidyverse/ellmer/issues/375

I've cobbled together a quick demo implementation of the protocol in R at [this gist](https://gist.github.com/simonpcouch/b8e9f07993b0f2c9f863d505f2c3005f).

I think, from the UI perspective, we're interested in folks being able to easily register + call tools from another MCP server, just as if they were ellmer tools? So, maybe:

```r
tools_from_some_server <- mcp_tools(some_connection_specification)

ch <- ellmer::chat_anthropic()
ch$set_tools(tools_from_some_server)
```

In the above, we literally translate the `"tools/list"` output from the server into an R list of ellmer tools that's compatible with the existing `set_tools()` implementation. Each of the `@fun` entries would be wrappers that just send the right json to the server. This approach (rather than `tools_from_some_server` having some special class) is also nice in that ellmer doesn't need to "know" about acquaint.

If this functionality does end up acquaint, it's probably worth once again reconsidering naming before the package goes "live."

title: Server remains running after client exits (Claude Desktop on MacOS)
description:
Not tested with other clients / platforms.

The MCP protocol at https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/lifecycle#stdio says:

> stdio
>
> For the stdio [transport](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/transports), the client SHOULD initiate shutdown by:
>
> First, closing the input stream to the child process (the server)
> Waiting for the server to exit, or sending SIGTERM if the server does not exit within a reasonable time
> Sending SIGKILL if the server does not exit within a reasonable time after SIGTERM
>
> The server MAY initiate shutdown by closing its output stream to the client and exiting.

So Claude Desktop is definitely not doing what it *should* do as there is nothing blocking SIGTERM. Perhaps the way it is worded, *may* provides an alternative, which seems to be what it's actually doing, which is just closing the output stream and exiting.

Fortunately, as in #16 I've bridged stdin to a nanonext socket, we're now able to catch such events.
